data.description:
Mickey Mouse's job is probably safe, but spare a thought for the thousands of Walt Disney employees on the wrong end of layoffs this year. At least investors have been doing well heading into Tuesday's fourth-quarter earnings report.

By George Glover

As harsh as it appears, slashing jobs has helped power the entertainment and theme park company's stock 29% higher since late March, to trade at just under $120 as of Thursday. Shares of Disney's rival Netflix are flat over the same period.

Pleasing investors has been a top priority for CEO Josh D'Amaro, who succeeded Bob Iger in March. He joined Disney nearly three decades ago and headed up Disney's experiences division from 2020 to 2026. He has hit the ground running thanks to the cost cuts, his grand plans for streaming, and a rock-solid parks business delivering about 60% of the company's profit.

Shares suffered a Tower of Terror-style plunge from February 2021 to December 2022, shedding half of their value due to concerns about Disney's TV networks, including sports channel ESPN. But former parks exec D'Amaro's strong start as CEO means the stock may finally be ready to rally. Should investors consider buying in?

Here's how he has done it.

Let's start with the layoffs. (The exact numbers aren't clear but are expected to be in the thousands.) D'Amaro has swung the ax at divisions including Pixar and ESPN since taking charge as he bids to streamline the sprawling company. Slashing expenses won't win him any internal popularity contests, but it's just what investors wanted.

"The stock has traded in a range for a really long time," Seaport Research Partners analyst David Joyce tells Barron's. Shares have been trapped at $79 to $120 since April 2022. "The market gave D'Amaro a couple of quarters to get comfortable, but now we've seen layoffs and head-count reductions, Disney is putting the profitability narrative into place."

The stock's recent rally isn't just about cost cuts. Price hikes and ad-supported plans have at last helped make Disney+ profitable, after years when the streaming platform lagged behind Netflix. Analysts polled by FactSet expect profit for Disney's entertainment division to grow by 21%, to $6.6 billion, over the next two years, with streaming more than offsetting declines in its linear TV businesses like ABC and ESPN.

D'Amaro, meanwhile, has big plans for streaming. He promised to go all-in on technology in a 3,000-word letter to shareholders back in May, laying out a plan to make Disney+ a one-stop shop where users can interact with all of the company's different businesses. The CEO wants to make the streaming service "more engaging, more personalized, and more central to how fans experience our brands." The vision is for users to be able to move seamlessly from old Disney movies to live sports broadcasts to park promotions, without ever leaving the platform.

Big swings are possible because Disney's experiences division, which covers parks and cruises, remains a reliable moneymaker. Even the Iran war hasn't dented demand — analysts estimate that operating income for the division rose 11%, to $11.1 billion, over the fiscal year ended in September.

Barron's drew up a to-do list for Disney back in January, and we'd give D'Amaro an A- if we were grading his time in charge so far. The new CEO has signaled that he'll accelerate streaming growth and build on parks' strong track record — but ESPN remains a worry. D'Amaro mentioned the sports cable channel 15 times in the letter to investors, without laying out a clear plan for how to offset cable losses.

But the good news is that Disney's legacy TV networks are no longer a Dumbo-size problem, largely because their profit has taken a beating over the past decade — and the market has given up trying to price them in. From 2022 to 2025, operating income for the TV division dropped to $2.96 billion from $8.52 billion.

"That should no longer be a reason for Disney to get punished," says Morningstar analyst Matt Dolgin. "It doesn't even matter anymore....This company shouldn't be trading on that at all."

He says a sum-of-the-parts model could value Disney at $155 a share, with the parks and cruises business worth $175 billion by itself. The company's total market cap stood at $207 billion as of Wednesday.

D'Amaro has already convinced investors that he has the magic touch. If the looming report tops the Street's expectations, shares will get the pixie dust they need to extend their strong recent run.

By Steven M. Sears

Artificial intelligence may destroy humanity, and data center opposition could decimate the AI ecosystem, but the Democrats who now control Congress are unlikely to severely impede progress. Even the most vehement protesters are likely to evolve their thinking.

AI is a national security concern, critical to the defense and advancement of America, and that almost certainly protects data centers from punitive legislation. AI also has the power to advance medicine and science and make the world a better place.

It is safe to assume Democrats and Republicans understand that weakening America's AI dominance benefits China and Russia. The respected, nonpartisan Congressional Research Service has explained that since at least 2020.

Despite campaign rodomontade and widespread protests, the new Democrat-controlled Congress will likely develop realistic data center legislation, rather than use its powers to stifle an important technology.

Investors should use current controversies — and all that will follow — to build positions that benefit from what will likely be a national data center policy that addresses concerns, including pollution and extreme water and electrical usage, without impeding the AI buildout.

The investor class abhors political challenges, but major innovations need regulatory frameworks that balance public and private good. A lawyer helping a private-equity firm with a South Carolina data center said he didn't understand why they wanted to build near a neighborhood rather than in nearby rural areas. He has a point.

Some states and areas will likely emerge as pro-data center, just as state and federal legislation should ultimately harmonize as controversies mature. Volatility in its many forms — political, social, and financial — will define the process and create many investment opportunities.

Even now, many data center stocks are stable, despite so many Prince Hamlet investors who are vacillating between AI's stunning promise and cost. Amazon.com, Meta Platforms, Microsoft, and Alphabet data center spending is either dismissed as the cost of business or as insanity. Still, the AI investment theme is here to stay.

Aggressive investors can consider Equinix. Third-quarter financial results were strong, and the data center company's guidance was robust. Equinix operates 282 data centers in 36 countries. More than 90% of revenue is recurring. The 50 largest customers generated 35% of recurring revenue in the third quarter. Less than 3% of recurring revenue over the past three years came from the largest customer.

While the company is dynamic, Equinix's stock and options trading aren't, and that requires creativity.

For every 100 Equinix shares that are bought, investors can sell a put and buy a call. The put sale pays you to buy more stock at a lower price, while the call increases in value as the stock advances.

Consider puts and calls that expire in one to two months, with strike prices that are within 5% of the stock price.

During the past 52 weeks, Equinix stock has ranged from $720.62 to $1,128.68. Shares are up about 37% this year, far more than the S&P 500 index, a fact that reinforces that data centers are far from dead despite the headlines and campaign rhetoric.

The data center investment is likely to be long-term rewarding but short-term trying, as it will take time for political and local controversies to find reasonable legislative expression.

Recommending data center investments, moreover, expresses a view that investors have overreacted and that wagers against AI and data centers are too pessimistic.

Still, a lot must fall into place. Data center supporters must become as effective as Chinese and Russian propagandists, who are surely using social media and other tools to influence American public opinion and politics.

America must win the AI race. Any other outcome endangers national security and global stability, and that's bad for everyone.
